title: Set a spring rat trap without letting its hammer snap
instruction: Set the rat trap, with its lock bar holding the hammer back, without ever letting the hammer snap and without a gripper in the hammer's path while nothing holds it back. Leave both grippers clear of the set trap and both arms back where they started.
context: Setting a wooden snap trap is a familiar household job when rats get into a house, garage or shed. The hammer's strong spring makes it fiddly, and a hammer that slips snaps down hard enough to hurt a finger, so people keep their fingers out of its path until the lock bar holds it. A home robot asked to deal with rats would face the same small job.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. A large wooden snap trap for rats is screwed to a pine plank (32 x 16 cm, 1.5 cm thick) lying across the centre line 27 cm forward. The trap's pine board is 22.5 x 9 cm and 1.1 cm thick, from 14 to 36.5 cm forward. Its U-shaped steel hammer (50 g, side arms of 6 mm wire 8 cm apart, a 10 mm steel cross bar 7.5 cm from the axle) turns on an axle 27 cm forward and 4.1 cm above the table. A spring pushes the hammer forward with about 0.3 N m when it is pulled right back. At the start, the hammer lies sprung forward over the yellow plastic trigger pedal, its cross bar 34.5 cm forward. The lock bar (8 mm square steel, 12.5 cm long, 20 g) is pinned on a steel staple post 15 cm forward and 1.5 cm left of the centre line. It stands up, leaning back against its stop. A brass catch sits beside the axle, 27.5 cm forward. With the hammer pulled back over to the near end, the lock bar lies level across it, and pressing the lock bar's tip down into the catch latches it there. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. 0.0 if the hammer ever snapped forward: swinging forward faster than 200 degrees a second once pulled back past 30 degrees, or set off by a gripper over the trigger pedal of the set trap. It is also 0.0 if a gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) or fingertips were ever in the hammer's strike path while nothing held the hammer back (the hammer pulled back past 30 degrees, no TCP within 3.5 cm of its cross bar, and the lock bar not yet latched). The strike path is 2.5 to 9.5 cm from the axle, within 5.5 cm of the trap's middle line, and more than 15 degrees ahead of the hammer. Otherwise 1.0: the trap set (the lock bar's tip latched in the catch and the hammer held at least 160 degrees back), each TCP at least 4 cm from the hammer's cross bar and the lock bar's tip, and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: the trap set; 0.25: the hammer pulled back at least 165 degrees at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the hammer and the lock bar still.
reset_notes: Lift the lock bar's tip out of the catch while holding the hammer, let the hammer down gently, and stand the lock bar back up against its stop.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the trap is screwed to a plank, so it cannot move. The hammer's coil spring is a hinge drive. The catch is a rule: when the hammer is pulled back and the lock bar's tip comes within 8 mm of the catch, the task file holds the lock bar where it is. There is no bait; the trigger pedal does not move, but a gripper over it releases the catch. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
